tags.gist: Supports all three approaches but says none, run periodically, can detect the within-session degradation measured; proposes triggers not tied to a calendar.
Reports degradation that occurred within a session and reset at its boundary, which any periodic re-benchmark would miss by starting a fresh session.
Says the working trigger is a gap between a device's reported actions and an independent record, measurable continuously rather than by elapsed time.
Notes the commenter has published an open-source independent record and marks which parts are verified and which are unmeasured design.
Says for users who cannot speak, something other than the user must catch fabrication and alert someone able to act.
Says re-benchmarking cannot see failures that grow with time inside a session, because every benchmark run starts a new session.
Says clinician review cannot mark fabricated reports as wrong from text, and sampling position determines the result when presentation improves while errors persist.
Would put the program's weight on degradation monitoring, but defined as a within-session function of time, turns and context rather than drift over weeks.
Proposes contemporaneous verification of a device's account against an independent machine-produced access record, which separates reading, stale copies and fabrication mechanically.
Describes the published open-source ledger that records running systems from the process list, offered as a method any regulator or manufacturer can apply.
Proposes writing the access record first and entering the device's account against it: self-reports become annotations on an independent record, never the record.
Would retain periodic cadence for what it does well but not let it carry the detection load.
Recommends continuous within-session evaluation reported by elapsed time and turn index, keeping re-benchmarking only to confirm criteria after changes.
Proposes five triggers computable without adjudication: claim-record divergence, silence, within-session thresholds, absence claims, and presentation diverging from accuracy.
Argues the triggers need no clinician or schedule and are cheaper to run continuously than quarterly re-benchmarking, serving least-burdensome aims.
Asks CDRH to require that detected fabrication or mistranslation for users who cannot self-verify notify a designated caregiver or clinician at session end.
Bounds that recommendation: it notifies a named person of a device fault, and is not surveillance or transmission of the user's communication.
Clarifies the measurements came from commercial assistants, not regulated devices, and establish that the failures occur, not how often.
Distinguishes the published, verifiable instrument from the unmeasured check-in design, noting the triggers depend only on an access record.
Recommends against any standard turning on candour or intent, since every proposed trigger is observable without resolving why an output occurred.
Says postmarket cadence and alert routing decide whether users without a second channel are protected; a quarterly report comes after harm.
